title: The five times
hookLine: dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset, night, and how the sun sets the clock

lines: YOU NEED A WINDOW, NOT A CLOCK.
cards: Day one hundred, and a day with five doors in it. The first opens while it's still dark, when the sky just starts to gray. The second, just after the sun passes its highest point.
The third, in the long afternoon, when shadows stretch. The fourth, right after the sun disappears. The fifth, when the last red light has gone from the sky.
You don't need a clock to find them. You need a window.

teach.b: The Qur'an says, in Surah an-Nisa, that prayer is enjoined on the believers at fixed times. The five are named from the day itself.

Fajr, dawn: from first light until sunrise. Dhuhr, midday: just after the sun passes its peak. Asr, afternoon: when a thing's shadow has grown to its own length, or in the Hanafi school, twice its length.
Maghrib, sunset: once the sun is gone. And Isha, night: when the twilight has faded. That's why prayer times change every day, and why a timetable in Oslo looks nothing like one in Nairobi.
The sun keeps the clock, not the watch. Why five? A hadith in Bukhari tells it as part of the Night Journey.
On the ascent, the Prophet ﷺ was given fifty prayers a day. On his way down, Musa stopped him and said, in effect, your people won't manage that, go back and ask for less.
He went back again and again, and it came down to five.
The hadith ends: five in the doing, fifty in the reward. Look where the times fall: waking, the middle of work, the afternoon slump, the end of the day, the edge of sleep.

teach.h: AT THE HINGES OF THE DAY.
teach.b: Five hinges of an ordinary day, and a prayer at each.
Shia practice allows joining them into three sittings, dawn, midday with afternoon, sunset with night, and Sunni schools allow joining on a journey. It's still five prayers.

how: Muslims pray five obligatory prayers a day, fajr, dhuhr, asr, maghrib and isha, at times set by the sun's position, and, because the times shift daily, they often check a printed timetable or an app.

o: the ritual prayer, made five times a day
the call to prayer sung from a mosque
any private prayer said in your own words

games.q: which prayer, which sky — tap the pairs.

s: prayer times are the same every day
they follow the sun, so they shift a little every day and differ from city to city.
a hadith says the prayers began as fifty and came down to five
on the Night Journey, with Musa urging the Prophet ﷺ to ask for less (Bukhari).
joining prayers into three sittings means praying only three
it's still five prayers; Shia practice allows praying them in three sittings.

games.q: you're coming down from the heavens on the Night Journey, carrying fifty prayers a day. Musa stops you. what does he say?
o: your people won't manage it; go back and ask for less
games.why: Musa sent him back again and again until it was five, and the hadith says: five in the doing, fifty in the reward.

practice: Look up today's five times where you are, from a prayer app, a mosque's website or a search, and read them slowly: fajr, dhuhr, asr, maghrib, isha.
Notice which have passed and which is next, then look out a window if you can and guess where the sun is on that path. If you pray, you can set a small reminder for the next one.

wordCard.voice: Salah, the obligatory prayer prescribed five times a day: fajr, dhuhr, asr, maghrib, isha, set by the sun, fifty that became five.

orig.note: Arabic: five prayers. salawat is the plural of salah, prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: the sun keeps the times. Five doors, and the light opens each one. One hundred days, and counting.
